lede: From Attila's court to the murder of Aetius, then the long afterlife. The chronicles rarely give a day; where the sources disagree, the station says so. Each linked station opens its passage.

stations.text: Aetius' general Litorius leads Hunnic auxiliaries against the Visigoths and is taken before Toulouse; Avitus renews the treaty with Theoderic. Twelve years later the same peoples are allies against the Huns.
The historian Priscus travels with an East Roman embassy to Attila and describes the wooden court, the banquet and the king as judge. His account survives in fragments; Jordanes quotes him.
Prosper says Attila announced he was marching only against the Goths, 'as a guardian of Roman friendship', and that many cities of Gaul felt his attack once he had crossed the Rhine.
Valentinian's embassy to Theoderic; Avitus brings the Goths; Aetius gathers Franks, Burgundians, Alans, Saxons, Armoricans and others. Sangiban the Alan is suspected of treason.

Gregory of Tours, on hearsay: the Huns reach Metz on the eve of Easter and burn it; only the oratory of Saint Stephen is left standing. A bishop of Tongres had been told in Rome that the invasion was God's sentence.

Gregory: bishop Anianus prays on the walls, and Aetius and Theoderic arrive as they are about to fall. The Life of Anianus: the Huns are already inside. Sidonius: the city was broken into but not plundered. A later Life gives 24 June.

Two later Lives: Lupus of Troyes, whose city had no walls, is taken by Attila as far as the Rhine; Genovefa keeps the Parisians from fleeing and is nearly stoned as a false prophet. Their editor Krusch judged both Lives late.

On the Catalaunian fields (Jordanes, Hydatius), 'not far from Metz' (Hydatius), or at Mauriacus five miles from Troyes (the Gallic sources). Theoderic falls; Attila withdraws into his wagon fort; Aetius advises Thorismud to go home, and Attila leaves Gaul. No source gives the day.
Raised on the battlefield, Thorismud returns to Toulouse. Jordanes says Aetius advised it for fear of the Goths; the Copenhagen continuation and Gregory say it was a trick to keep the spoils.

Attila takes Aquileia (Jordanes' storks), Milan and Pavia; Pope Leo meets him on the Mincio, and he turns back. Prosper blames Aetius for leaving the Alps open; Hydatius credits famine, disease and an army from the East.
After his wedding to Ildico, Attila dies of a haemorrhage in the night, Jordanes says after Priscus; Marcellinus says a woman stabbed him. His sons divide the peoples and lose them.
Ardaric the Gepid leads the subject peoples against Attila's sons; Ellac falls, and 'the Huns gave way, to whom the whole world was thought to give way'.
Valentinian III kills Aetius with his own hand in the palace in 454; in 455 Aetius' guardsmen kill Valentinian. Marcellinus: 'with him fell the Western realm'.
Chapter 35 of the Decline and Fall: 'the last victory which was achieved in the name of the Western empire', decided by 'the blind impetuosity of Barbarians'.
Edward Creasy puts Châlons among his Fifteen Decisive Battles of the World: Gibbon's 'last victory' becomes the saving of 'the Germanic element in the civilization of modern Europe'.

At Bremerhaven Wilhelm II sends troops to China: 'Pardon wird nicht gegeben'. The press version compares them to the Huns under Etzel; the official text leaves the Huns out. In 1914 the British call the Germans 'Huns'.
Kipling's poem in The Times, a month into the war: Attila's name, by way of the Kaiser's speech, becomes the name for Germans.
